sources.title: Tesla turns to 50-year-old stunt technology as it tries to Roadster again

discussion.body: Silly, but effective: the pipes exist to make the gas jets look like something a combustion car would do. The whole gesture is an admission that the interesting part of a car show is the noise and the fire, and that you can fake both with nitrogen.

The mundane questions are left dangling. Ars Technica's writer notes that he has yet to locate the section of the Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Statutes explaining how and when such a device would be legal to use on the road.

items.title: The New Tesla Roadster's Party Trick: 100,000-psi Nitrogen, Fired Out of Four Fake Exhaust Pipes
items.body: Nine years after Tesla first tried to resurrect the Roadster, the company is apparently trying again, Ars Technica reports. At the rear of the new car sit four giant exhaust pipes — which, no, do not signal a sudden embrace of hydrocarbons. They are where jets of compressed nitrogen at 100,000 psi shoot out. That is the spec sheet's most memorable line, and it tells you what kind of object this is. A car whose defining feature is a compressed-gas launcher is not really being sold as transportation; it is stage equipment, and the pipes are the costume.

sources.title: Francis Lawrence To Direct Sci-Fi Film ‘Red Rising’ For Paramount

items.title: Paramount Buys 'Red Rising,' With Francis Lawrence Directing the First Book
items.body: Paramount has acquired the film rights to Pierce Brown's New York Times bestselling science-fiction series Red Rising and has enlisted Francis Lawrence to direct an adaptation of the first installment, Deadline reports. Justin Rhodes, whose credits include Terminator: Dark Fate and the Prime Video series Secret Level, will write the script. The deal is for a series, but the announcement only commits Paramount to book one. Buying the rights is the easy half; the first film has to earn the rest, which makes the director-writer pairing the entire bet.

sources.title: “thegentlemanpervert” producing AI CSAM is a NJ prosecutor, say cops

discussion.body: The Justice Department's stated position predates this case. After charging a Wisconsin man in 2024 with spreading thousands of realistic images of children across Telegram and Instagram, the department clarified to law enforcement that CSAM generated by AI is still CSAM.
The alleged starting point is what makes this concrete rather than abstract: not an invented face, but a photograph of a real child. The generation step changes the medium, not the subject.

items.title: A New Jersey Prosecutor Is Charged Over AI-generated Abuse Material
items.body: New Jersey's deputy attorney general, Brian Richard Fitzgerald, was arrested on felony charges related to AI-generated child sexual abuse material, Bucks County Detectives said. New Jersey officials accused the 51-year-old of using AI to make photos from social media of real minors into sexualized images that he then distributed on social media. The striking part is the defendant: a serving deputy attorney general is the one facing the charges.

sources.title: ‘Crypto King’ spent $16.3M of investor funds on cars, credit cards, jets, security, accountant testifies

items.title: Nearly Half of the 'Crypto King's' Investor Money Went to Him, Accountant Testifies
items.body: A senior forensic accountant testified Friday in Toronto's Superior Court that Aiden Pleterski — the self-described “Crypto King” — spent nearly half of the $36.3 million investors gave him on himself, CBC reports, and paid out about the same amount to investors as returns between 2020 and 2022. Put the two figures side by side and most of the money is accounted for: one large slice to personal spending, another to the payouts that kept funds coming in. A payout pipeline and a personal budget are not an investment strategy, and the gap between them is the thing a courtroom gets to sort out.

sources.title: ‘I Play Rocky’ Surprise Screens at London Film Festival

discussion.body: Casting a relative newcomer as a face this famous is the entire bet of a film like this. If the audience doesn't buy the impression, nothing else in the movie can rescue it.
The praise so far comes from a friendly setting — a surprise screening introduced by the director, who used the moment to shout out his own lead. That's a first test, not a verdict.

items.title: London's Surprise Slot Went to the Making of Rocky
items.body: Variety reported that the London Film Festival's surprise film on Friday night was I Play Rocky, Peter Farrelly's biographical drama about the beginnings of Sylvester Stallone's boxing franchise. Farrelly was on hand to introduce it and shouted out his star, newcomer Anthony Ippolito, who has already earned praise for his portrayal of Stallone. A film about the making of a famous film lives or dies on whether you believe the impression, and a festival introduction is where that gamble gets its first public airing.

sources.title: Conduct of Monetary Policy under Housing Market Imbalances

discussion.body: The demand-versus-supply distinction is doing a lot of work here. The same shelter inflation figure could point toward quite different policy depending on where it came from.
Suppose the two really do call for different responses — what does a central bank do while the origin of a rent spike is still unsettled?
The note's own list of drivers — house prices, mortgage costs, rents, supply constraints, leverage — suggests the origins are tangled together rather than cleanly separated.

items.title: When Rent Drives the Inflation Number, Should a Central Bank Look Through It?
items.body: A Bank of Canada note starts from a Canadian fact: housing imbalances have elevated shelter inflation as a driver of the consumer price index, fuelled by high house prices, mortgage costs, rents, supply constraints and leverage. Shelter — what people pay to live somewhere — is not a quirky line item you can quietly ignore when it starts pushing the headline number around. The note's question is whether monetary policy should incorporate shelter inflation or look through it: respond to it, or treat it as something that will pass on its own. What makes the question hard is that the answer may depend on the shock's origin. The authors build a model with housing supply and extrapolative expectations — expectations that project recent price behaviour forward — to assess incorporating versus looking through under demand shocks and supply shocks separately.

sources.title: How Alaska became a key battleground in the fight for the Senate

items.title: Alaska's Senate Debate: Fuel Costs and a Staffing Allegation
items.body: PBS NewsHour reports that Alaska could play a pivotal role in Democrats' efforts to reclaim control of the Senate. At a debate, Republican incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan faced questions about rising fuel costs driven by the war with Iran, while Democratic challenger Mary Peltola pushed back against allegations that she mistreated staff members. A state where energy prices and a personal-conduct charge are both on the table is one where a single debate can carry two unrelated arguments at once.

sources.title: Albania: Students demand political change and resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama

items.title: Empty Lecture Halls and Burning Buildings: Albania's Student Protests
items.body: Deutsche Welle reports that Albanian students are spearheading a protest movement — empty lecture halls, burning buildings and demands for change — which it describes as the biggest challenge to Prime Minister Edi Rama in years. When the pressure comes from people who are supposed to be sitting in classrooms rather than from the usual party machinery, the institution they are meant to be inside becomes the site of the objection.

sources.title: Beyond "Looking Through": Monetary Policy Responses and Communication Under Supply-Driven Inflation

discussion.body: Notice that the paper does not pose this as look-through versus no look-through. Both rules respond to inflation; the difference is a matter of degree, which makes 'how far do you look through' a dial rather than a switch.

If that's right, the size of the response may be the less interesting coefficient. Pairing each rule with a different information protocol suggests the explanation the bank gives could do work the response itself cannot — which is a hypothesis worth testing, not a conclusion the design settles.

items.title: Lean Against or Look Through: The Bank of Canada Runs Both Inflation Rules
items.body: When inflation moves, a central bank has to decide how hard to push back. A Bank of Canada paper describes a controlled macroeconomic experiment built around exactly that decision, comparing policy rules that differ in how much they look through inflation: a Lean-Against policy with a strong response, and a Look-Through policy with a weaker one. Same economy, two temperaments — one that treats a price spike as something to fight, one that treats it as something to tolerate while the reaction works through the system elsewhere. Questions about how aggressively to respond are usually argued in prose; the point of a controlled experiment is to make the difference in response strength the variable being changed on purpose rather than the thing being disputed after the fact. The design also refuses to treat a central bank as a silent hand on the lever. Each rule is paired with communication protocols that vary how much information the bank releases about its policy response, which allows the strength of the reaction and the explanation of it to be studied separately rather than bundled together.

sources.title: Chase Infiniti-Starring ‘The Julia Set’ Acquired By Sony Pictures Classics After TIFF Premiere

items.title: A Student Drama From TIFF Lands at Sony Pictures Classics
items.body: Sony Pictures Classics has taken U.S. and key international territory rights to The Julia Set, the student drama starring Chase Infiniti and directed by Niki Byrne. Deadline reports the film drew headlines at the Toronto Film Festival as Infiniti's next feature outing following One Battle After Another, which the outlet describes as multi-Oscar winning. So the trajectory here is a festival premiere, a lead coming off a heavily awarded film, and a specialty distributor buying in for North America plus key international markets — a small film carrying a recognizable name rather than a large one pretending to be small.

sources.title: Inside Ukrainian offensive pushing Russia back - with Starlink playing a key role

items.title: Ukraine's Operation Vivaldi Regains Ground in the Donbas
items.body: The BBC joined Ukraine's Operation Vivaldi as it regained crucial territory in the Donbas. The same reporting notes that optimism around the push has been dampened by souring relations with President Trump. Ground recovered and political support are being read together rather than as separate stories — the battlefield result and the diplomatic weather arriving in the same dispatch.

sources.title: High-profile legionnaire apologizes following profanity-laced outburst at Carbonear, N.L., wedding reception

items.title: A Legion Wedding in Carbonear, Interrupted Before the Bouquet
items.body: A wedding reception at the Royal Canadian Legion branch in Carbonear, N.L., ended earlier this month in an angry outburst. CBC reports that high-profile legionnaire and veteran Berkley Lawrence confronted the bride as she prepared to throw her wedding bouquet. The setting and the timing are what make it a story: a Legion hall reception is about as conventional as a wedding gets, and the bouquet toss is the most ceremonial minute of the night — the part nobody expects to become a confrontation.

sources.title: The Best Horror Movies of 2026 (So Far), Ranked: ‘Obsession,’ ‘Resident Evil,’ ‘Backrooms’ and More

discussion.body: The interesting column here is the cheap one. Few genres still let a modest original sit in the same conversation as a known name, and Variety puts Backrooms and Obsession right next to the sequels.

Two different claims are being blended there: box office performance and the quality verdict. Variety's evidence for the hits is commercial; the good-to-great judgment is critical. A year can score on one and not the other.

items.title: Horror's 2026 So Far: Cheap Hits in One Column, Sequels Variety Could Have Skipped in the Other
items.body: Variety's running tally of 2026 horror describes a wild year, and the shape of it is a split: low-budget box office hits such as Backrooms and Obsession on one side, sequels the trade paper says the world could have lived without — Scream 7 and The Strangers – Chapter 3 — on the other. A list that puts those four titles in the same breath is making an argument about what audiences rewarded versus what they merely recognized in a poster, though Variety frames the sequel half only as a shrug, not a box office verdict, and the only numbers it offers are built into the phrase “low-budget hits.” The overall assessment is warmer than that split suggests: a year loaded with scary movies, many of them good-to-great, a welcome surprise that kept multiplexes busy. Horror keeps being the genre where a first-time idea and a franchise installment can share a marquee, and Variety's list ranks the standouts rather than sorting them by budget.

sources.title: Cause of fiery Calgary bus crash that killed 3 passengers, injured 16 under investigation

items.title: Calgary Police Are Still Working Out Why a City Bus Crashed and Burned
items.body: Three passengers died and 16 other people were hurt in a fiery Calgary city bus crash, and police are still working to determine what caused it. Among the injured is a police officer who helped save a child. Global News reports the investigation is ongoing.

sources.title: Oregon school shooter attacked special education classroom, police say

items.title: Bend Police Investigate Motive in Elementary School Shooting
items.body: Four people were killed at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon, police say, including three young children and a teacher. The shooter, identified by police as a 16-year-old who previously attended the school, attacked a special education classroom before being killed at the scene. Police say they are still investigating the motive.

sources.title: How Itaú is building generative AI for its entire customer base

items.title: Itaú's AI Push Comes With a Chat Window in Front and a Governance Platform Behind
items.body: OpenAI's account of its work with Itaú names two pieces of the same strategy: ia.i, a conversational interface for customers, and IARA, a governance platform. The bank is applying an “AI First” approach across customers and employees, in what OpenAI calls one of Brazil's most regulated sectors. The pairing is the part worth noticing. A customer-facing assistant is the visible product; a governance layer is the machinery that decides what the assistant is allowed to do, which is the piece a bank in a heavily regulated market cannot leave implicit. Because this is the vendor describing its own customer's deployment, read the architecture as design intent rather than a demonstrated result. Whether the guardrails hold under real traffic is a question an outside evaluation would answer, not a case study.

sources.title: Alex Gibney on How a CGI Avatar Helped Simulate the Elon Musk Interview He Could Never Get

discussion.body: A likeness does the work a real subject's silence would otherwise do. It lets the film press its case with nobody in the room able to refuse a question or correct an answer.
The film was already choosing who to leave out; a simulation just puts one of those choices on screen where it can be seen, instead of leaving it buried in the edit.

items.title: Alex Gibney's 'Musk' Simulates an Interview With a CGI Avatar
items.body: When a documentary subject won't sit for an interview, the filmmaker has to decide what goes in the gap. In 'Musk,' Alex Gibney's answer was for the production team to simulate an interview with Elon Musk using a CGI avatar. Gibney discussed that choice on IndieWire's Screen Talk podcast, along with who the film had to leave out. Both are telling choices in the same direction: an interview the film never obtained, and people the film had to set aside — the material that isn't there becomes part of the construction rather than a hole in it. A reconstruction can be the most candid option available when the camera can't get into the room. What a simulated interview doesn't give an audience is anything to check the performance against: no hesitation, no eye contact, nothing that belonged to the person being portrayed. The result is an interview-shaped scene with no interviewee behind it.

sources.title: Julianne Moore and Paul Giamatti Were So ‘Perfect’ in ‘The Debut’ That They Cut Shooting Time Short

items.title: Jesse Eisenberg Says Every Scene in 'The Debut' Is a First or Second Take
items.body: At the Middleburg Film Festival, filmmaker Jesse Eisenberg told the audience that every scene used in his latest film, 'The Debut' comes from his leads' first and second take. Julianne Moore, who stars in the film, joined him for the conversation. That's a statement about acting and editing at once: the performance kept is the one from the floor, not the one found after a dozen more attempts. Festival audiences only ever get the surviving take, which in this case is the early one.

sources.title: A federal IVF program will harmonize ‘patchwork’ approach, experts say

items.title: 46% of Canadians With an Opinion Back the Proposed Federal IVF Program
items.body: An Ipsos survey conducted for Fertility Matters Canada found that 46 per cent of Canadians with an opinion on the subject support the proposed federal IVF funding program. The qualifier is the story: that's 46 per cent of the people who expressed a view, not 46 per cent of Canadians.

sources.title: Trial of German steakhouse heiress that sparked a huge spy scandal

items.title: Fifteen Months of Hearings, and a Charge of Ordering Her Children's Abduction
items.body: The BBC reports that for 15 months a high-security courtroom in Hamburg has been hearing the case of Christina Block, who is accused of ordering the abduction of her children. She has not been convicted; the case is the accusation and the courtroom built around it, not a verdict — indeed, the long record of hearings is what the report conveys about where the matter stands now, more than a year in with no resolution there to see in it — the duration itself being the only concrete fact on offer beyond the charge, which is the strange part. Abduction is the word usually attached to strangers; here it is alleged against a parent, and the proceedings are being conducted in a courtroom secured for the purpose. Fifteen months of hearings on a single accusation says something about how slowly a case of this shape moves through the courts.
